reason: E1 confirms that misfit volumes, elastic constants, and stacking fault energies are accessible via first-principles and are inputs for strengthening/ductility models, supporting premises 1 and 2. E3 states ML can exceed 90% prediction accuracy, supporting premise 3, and notes that CALPHAD and ab initio are resource-intensive, partially supporting premise 4. However, no cited evidence quantifies the baseline accuracy of 70-90% for strength metrics or supports the claimed 5-10× efficiency gain and 5-10% accuracy improvement (premise 5), which is a significant overstatement.
premises: Physics-based descriptors (misfit volumes, elastic constants, stacking fault energies) can be extracted from first-principles calculations for disordered multi-principal element alloys.
These descriptors are sufficient inputs for models that predict strengthening and ductility.
Machine learning can accurately predict HEA properties when trained on appropriate data, achieving >90% accuracy.
Existing high-throughput DFT and CALPHAD methods are computationally demanding and have limited accuracy for strength-related metrics (70-90%).
A hybrid physics-ML workflow can achieve 5-10× efficiency gains and 5-10% accuracy improvements over prior methods.
